opus-5.5.text:
When I started Taichi as a PhD student at MIT, open source felt almost like a default. You build something useful, you put it out there, people use it, and that's the reward. In academia that works beautifully: citations, collaborators, students who pick up your work and take it further.

When we tried to build a company around it, my view got more nuanced, and honestly a bit more humbling. Open source is fantastic for adoption and credibility. It brings in brilliant contributors and makes people trust your technology because they can see the code. But adoption isn't revenue. Many developers loved the project and would star it on GitHub, but that doesn't mean anyone would pay for it. The open-core playbook works for some infrastructure companies, but it requires a very specific market shape. You need enterprises with a pain point serious enough that they'll pay for support, hosting, or extra features. For a graphics and simulation programming language, that bridge from community love to a business was much harder than I expected.

So I now see open source as a strategic tool rather than a business model by itself. It's great for building a community, recruiting, establishing technical leadership, and lowering the barrier for people to try something new. But as a founder you have to be clear from day one about where the value capture happens. If you can't answer what you're selling and who's paying, then open source just makes you very popular and very poor.

With Meshy, we took a different approach. We focus on a product that solves a concrete problem for users, generating 3D content, and people pay for that directly. I still deeply value open source. A lot of what we build depends on the open research community, and I'm proud of what Taichi became. But I've learned to separate two questions: what's good for the ecosystem, and what keeps the company alive. Ideally they align, but when they don't, a startup has to survive first. Otherwise you don't get to contribute anything to anyone.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim about marketing spending matching product development spending.

r005.rationale: It says users trust the technology because they can see the code.

r006.rationale: It says founders need to identify where value capture happens and describes selling a product users pay for directly.

r007.rationale: The speaker says they value open source, but does not suggest that a founder’s personal ideal can pull the company back toward open source.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's changed a lot. When I started Taichi as a research project at MIT, open source was almost the whole point. The goal was to let people write high-performance graphics and physics simulation code in a few lines of Python, and the way you get adoption for something like that is to put it out there, let people try it, and let the community tell you what's broken. The GitHub stars, the contributors, the folks building things on top of it — that was the feedback loop, and it was incredibly motivating. For a researcher, that's success.

Then we formed a company around it, and I had to confront a question I'd been avoiding: open source is a great way to build a community, but it's not a business model by itself. Stars don't pay salaries. A lot of people who love your project will never pay you a cent, and that's fine, that's how it should work — but you need to know where the actual value creation happens. Early on I think I conflated "people are using this" with "this is a company." Those aren't the same thing.

So my view today is more layered. Open source is still fundamental for infrastructure — compilers, programming languages, runtimes. Nobody wants to bet their product on a closed black box from a small startup. Being open is how you earn trust, and it's how you hire, because the best engineers often find you through the project. But a startup has to be very deliberate about what sits on top of that open core. What is the thing enterprises actually need that the open project doesn't give them? Reliability, support, integrations, a managed experience, solving the last-mile problem for a specific industry. That's where you focus the company's resources, while the open source part stays genuinely open and genuinely good.

The other lesson is about focus. An open source community pulls you in a hundred directions, because everyone has their own use case. That's healthy for the project but dangerous for a startup, which has to say no to almost everything. Learning to separate "what's good for the community" from "what's good for the business," and being honest with both groups about which is which, that's probably the biggest shift in how I think about it.

r001.rationale: The response says open source is not a business model by itself, but does not identify giving away the company’s best work as the source of monetization difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says the project helps with hiring because the best engineers often find the company through it.

r003.rationale: It describes open source as supporting adoption and community feedback, but does not frame development as marketing through R&D.

r004.rationale: The response makes no claim about marketing expenditure matching product development expenditure.

r005.rationale: It says being open earns trust and explains that users do not want to rely on a small startup’s closed black box.

r006.rationale: It says open source is not a business model by itself and that the startup must deliberately commercialize complementary offerings such as support, integrations, or a managed experience.

r007.rationale: The response describes a shift from a research project to a company, but does not say that the founder’s personal commitment to open source pulls the company back toward it.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more deliberate about what open source can do for a startup. It’s a great way to let people try your technology, learn from their feedback, and build trust. But having people use an open-source project doesn’t automatically mean you have a business. You still need to understand what problem matters enough that someone will pay you to solve it.

So I see open source as part of the strategy, rather than the strategy itself. What do you make open? What do you charge for? And how does the success of the community help sustain the company—and vice versa? Ideally, those things reinforce each other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more pragmatic about it. Open source can be a great way to share technology, get feedback, and build trust with developers. But in a startup, you also have to ask what makes the business sustainable. If people find your project useful, that doesn’t automatically mean you have a product they’ll pay for.

So I see open source as part of the strategy. You need to understand what you want to make broadly accessible, what customers need beyond that, and how the two support each other. And you have to take the community seriously, because maintaining an open-source project is a commitment.
